candidates.hypothesis: Adding the development sentiment contrast to the positive output row and subtracting it from the negative row should strengthen class-dependent margins and correct some near-boundary errors. A small coefficient limits disruption to the tied input embeddings, including label words in the prompt.

The initial contrast edit improved accuracy and NLL but shifted many positive examples toward negative. Increasing contrast strength while slightly scaling the positive row should strengthen sentiment separation and compensate for the contrast's negative midpoint projection. Because embeddings are tied, evaluation also measures changes to prompt representations.

Candidate 1 improves development accuracy but its positive-row scaling flips several negative reviews to positive. Keeping the contrast coefficients at ±0.2 while reducing positive-row scaling from 1.035 to 1.025 should recover some of those negative examples while preserving most corrected positive margins. Tied embeddings make this an empirical test of both output margins and prompt representation changes.

The stronger contrast in candidates 1 and 2 overcorrects some reviews whose original sentiment margins were reliable. Returning to contrast coefficients of ±0.1 while scaling the positive row by 1.025 should retain corrections from candidate 0 and recover positive reviews affected by the contrast's negative midpoint. The selective row scaling changes the decision boundary; tied input embedding effects are included in evaluation.

An intermediate contrast strength of ±0.15 with positive-row scale 1.03 may preserve candidate 3's reliable original margins while capturing more of candidate 1's class separation and lower NLL. This selective edit changes the sentiment decision boundary; evaluation includes its effects on the tied prompt embeddings.

Candidate 3 has the best development accuracy. Reducing its contrast coefficient to ±0.075 should recover original margins on positive reviews that project negatively onto the contrast, while retaining enough contrast to correct several baseline negative-review errors. Keeping positive-row scaling at 1.025 maintains the useful decision-boundary shift. Evaluation includes changes to the tied input embeddings.

Candidate 3's positive-row boost improves accuracy, but tied embeddings also alter the prompt. Applying a comparable boundary shift by reducing the negative row instead may preserve useful positive-token representations and correct additional mistakes. Contrast coefficients remain at ±0.1 to retain candidate 3's sentiment separation; this tests the distinct input effects of the alternative selective scaling.

Candidate 3 leaves several positive reviews just below the decision boundary. Raising only its positive-row scale from 1.025 to 1.0325 should correct some of those margins while retaining most negative-review margins. Keeping contrast coefficients at ±0.1 preserves its useful class separation; evaluation also captures tied input-embedding effects.

Increasing candidate 3's contrast coefficients modestly to ±0.125 while retaining positive-row scale 1.025 should correct its narrowly misclassified negative romance review and strengthen other negative margins. The smaller increase than candidate 4 may preserve more original positive margins. Evaluation includes effects on tied input embeddings.

Candidate 8 improves development accuracy but its positive-row boost flips several negative reviews with small margins. Reducing that scale to 1.02 while keeping contrast coefficients at ±0.125 may recover those reviews while preserving most corrected positive predictions. Evaluation includes the tied input-embedding effects.

Increasing candidate 9's contrast strength to ±0.15 while retaining positive-row scale 1.02 may recover additional negative reviews near the boundary and reduce NLL through stronger class-dependent margins. It may also lose positive reviews with negative contrast projections; evaluation includes tied input-embedding effects.

Reducing candidate 9's contrast strength slightly to ±0.1125 while retaining positive-row scale 1.02 may preserve original margins on reviews harmed by the contrast, while retaining corrections to baseline negative-review errors. This tests a weaker class-dependent decision-boundary adjustment, including its effects on tied input embeddings.
